Wythoff's Nim

Game StrategySequencesLogic
Game: Take counters from the two heaps; the player who takes the very last counter wins.
How to play: Click a square to remove it and every square to its right. Choose "two heaps" to take the same number from both at once.
Max heap size 15
Remove from
Look for the math

Two heaps and a simple rule hide a surprising pattern. Some pairs of heap sizes are safe to leave for the next player: whatever they take, you can answer. The computer is trying to leave exactly those pairs.

The pairs to leave behind

Starting at zero, the safe pairs are (1, 2), (3, 5), (4, 7), (6, 10), (8, 13) and so on. Their smaller number is floor(k × φ) and their larger number is that plus k, where φ ≈ 1.618 is the golden ratio. The difference between the two heaps is always k, so a pair is named by that difference. This is Wythoff's game, a cousin of Nim.

Why the pairs are safe

From a pair (a, a + k), taking from just one heap changes the difference, and taking the same number from both leaves the difference k but makes the smaller heap less than a: either way the pair is broken. From any other position there is a move back to a pair, which is why the computer keeps finding one. The two sequences of smaller and larger numbers fit together without gaps — a Beatty sequence pair — so every heap size belongs to exactly one pair.

What the applet really plays

The "one heap" and "two heaps" buttons limit which moves you may make, but the computer always uses the full-game pair table. Its table has four mistakes at the end: it lists (32, 53), (33, 56), (35, 60), (37, 63) where the correct pairs are (32, 52), (33, 54), (35, 57), (37, 60). The logic test computes the true pairs from scratch, checks them against the formula, and compares this port's computer with a second transcription of the applet's own code on every board up to 40 counters. It also confirms the applet's odd habit of giving the second heap 3 counters even when the maximum is 1 or 2.

Try a heap of 3 and a heap of 5. Can you find any first move that leaves the computer with no good answer?
